strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: joint 3D audio-visual grounding combining RGB-D and multi-channel FOA in an end-to-end learned AV-LLM, rather than modular/cascaded pipelines like SAVVY.

Introduces a reasonably novel Neural IV representation that replaces STFT-based intensity vectors with a learnable CNN-based encoder, and shows consistent gains over Classical IV, especially in overlapping-source and cross-scenario generalization settings (Table 3).

Contributes a large-scale (61k) synthetic dataset, SpatialSceneQA, with tightly synchronized RGB-D, 4-channel FOA, and fine-grained 3D annotations spanning perception and reasoning tasks, filling a real gap given the scarcity of such data (e.g., STARSS23 lacks aligned depth).

Fairly comprehensive ablations (depth encoding, FOA encoder, IV variant) that isolate the contribution of each architectural component and support the claim that explicit 3D/spatial modeling is necessary.
Clear and detailed architecture and data pipeline descriptions (simulation stages, coordinate conventions, task definitions) that aid reproducibility if code/data are released as promised.
weaknesses: The dataset and evaluation are entirely synthetic (SoundSpaces 2.0 / HM3D simulated scenes with LibriSpeech speech and synthetic loudspeaker meshes); there is no evaluation on real-world spatial audio-visual data (e.g., STARSS23), leaving open whether results transfer beyond simulation, despite the framing implying broader 'physical environment' applicability.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat unfair/incomplete: BAT uses binaural audio (converted via HRTF) rather than native FOA, N3D-VLM and Qwen3-VL are RGB(-D) only and evaluated zero-shot without fine-tuning on the new tasks, making it hard to isolate whether JAEGER's gains stem from the proposed architecture versus simply from more training data/tasks tailored to this benchmark.

The very high reasoning accuracies (99.2%-99.5%) and their near-total collapse without FOA (43-47%) suggest the reasoning tasks (D/E) may be somewhat easy/near-degenerate given only 2-3 discrete candidate speakers per scene; accuracy alone with few classes may not sufficiently demonstrate robust spatial reasoning versus superficial pattern matching from strong DoA cues.

Task C (3D IoU of only 0.32) shows relatively weak absolute grounding performance despite explicit depth encoding, but the paper does not sufficiently discuss why IoU remains modest or provide failure-mode analysis; the visual-offset metric alone may mask systematic size/orientation errors.

The dataset's audio realism is limited: only single-speaker LibriSpeech dry speech convolved with simulated RIRs, no ambient noise, environmental sounds, or diverse acoustic categories beyond speech, which may limit generalization claims made in the introduction about 'complex 3D environments' broadly.
Limited discussion of computational cost, inference latency, and scalability of Neural IV/depth encoding relative to Classical IV or RGB baselines, which matters for practical adoption.

No qualitative failure case analysis or error breakdown (e.g., by source distance, reverberation level, room type) is provided, limiting insight into when/why the model fails, especially for the still-large overlapping-source DoA error (13.13°).
Code, model checkpoints, and dataset are only promised 'upon acceptance,' so reproducibility cannot currently be independently verified.

strengths: Addresses a clearly articulated and underexplored gap: unifying RGB-D visual geometry with multi-channel (FOA) spatial audio for end-to-end 3D audio-visual grounding and reasoning in a single learned AV-LLM, rather than a cascaded pipeline (as in SAVVY) or RGB-only/single-source setups (as in Hear You Are).

The Neural IV component is well-motivated (STFT-based classical intensity vectors are brittle under reverberation/overlap) and is validated with a clean cross-evaluation matrix (Table 3) showing much better generalization across matched/mismatched single- vs overlap-source training regimes.

SpatialSceneQA is a substantial, carefully engineered dataset (61k samples) with a clear, reproducible synthesis pipeline (HM3D + SoundSpaces 2.0 + Hunyuan3D-generated loudspeakers), fine-grained degree-level azimuth/elevation and metric 3D box annotations, and disjoint train/val/test splits at the scene, speaker, and loudspeaker-asset level to test generalization.

Extensive and thoughtful ablations, including several appendix studies proactively addressing likely reviewer concerns: a matched-input SimpleFuse baseline isolating architectural contribution from modality access, FOA-vs-binaural comparison, a harder multi-candidate reasoning setting to show the main benchmark is not trivially saturated, and a small real-world STARSS23 sanity check.

Clear ablation of individual components (depth encoding, FOA encoder) on reasoning tasks demonstrating that removing FOA causes catastrophic performance collapse, supporting the core motivating claim about the necessity of 3D/spatial audio modeling.
Good methodological transparency: coordinate system explicitly defined, training/optimization details (LoRA config, per-task fine-tuning strategy, hardware) reported for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is entirely built on one simulator/scene-source combination (HM3D + SoundSpaces + LibriSpeech read speech + synthetic loudspeaker meshes); the only real-world check (Appendix A, STARSS23) is very small (753 clips) and shows azimuth errors remain extremely large (74-95°), which is a large enough gap to call into question how much of the reported 2-4° performance reflects genuine spatial-audio understanding versus overfitting to simulator-specific acoustic/rendering artifacts.

Many headline reasoning results are near-ceiling (99%+ accuracy), and the paper's own harder multi-candidate ablation (Appendix D) shows accuracy dropping sharply (e.g., Neural IV from 95% to 72.5%) with more distractors trained on only 160 samples, suggesting the main benchmark's near-ceiling numbers may partly reflect a constrained/simplified problem setting (2-3 candidates, template-like QA) rather than robust spatial reasoning; this undercuts the strength of the central claims.

Several baseline comparisons in Table 2 are architecturally guaranteed to fail (e.g., Qwen2.5-Omni cannot do DoA due to monaural-only input, N3D-VLM/Qwen3-VL lack any audio grounding pathway), making the headline 'necessity of 3D' claim partly a comparison against models that structurally cannot attempt the task rather than a fair ablation of the proposed 3D design versus a comparably resourced 2D system.

The core methodological contributions (3D positional encoding via depth back-projection, dual-path semantic/spatial audio separation, LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-Omni backbone) largely recombine existing techniques from cited prior works (Zheng et al. 2025, Wang et al. 2025, Tang et al. 2024); the main new element is the Neural IV, which is a reasonably incremental design (CNN + elementwise product + MLP in place of STFT cross-spectrum) rather than a fundamentally new representation.

No assessment of whether fine-tuning with LoRA and randomly initialized audio adapters degrades JAEGER's original general-purpose (non-spatial) omni capabilities inherited from Qwen2.5-Omni, so it's unclear whether the model remains a general AV-LLM or becomes narrowly specialized to the synthetic benchmark.

Test-set diversity is limited (36 HM3D test scenes, 12 held-out loudspeaker meshes), and no variance/error bars are reported across runs for the reported accuracies and MAEs, making it hard to judge the statistical reliability of small differences (e.g., 99.5% vs 98.6%) between compared variants.
